draft.title: Power functions
card: A power function has the form y = xⁿ, where n can be negative or a fraction. Its graph is shaped by values it cannot reach.

x cannot be 0, so the y-axis is a vertical asymptote, a line the graph approaches but never touches. y = 0 is a horizontal asymptote. For y = 1/x the branches are in opposite quadrants. For y = 1/x² both branches are above the x-axis.
y = √x needs x ≥ 0, so the graph starts at the point (0, 0) and rises to the right. It has no part to the left of the y-axis.
Example: y = 1/x has no point at x = 0. When x = 2, y = 1/2. When x = −2, y = −1/2.
draft.remember: The values a power function cannot use, such as x = 0 for 1/x or negative x for √x, set its shape.

a.q: Which statement is true for the graph of y = 1/x²?
opts: It has the y-axis as an asymptote and lies above the x-axis
It has the y-axis as an asymptote and dips below the x-axis
It passes through the origin and lies above the x-axis
It starts at the origin and has no part for negative x
a.why: x = 0 is not allowed, so the y-axis is an asymptote. Squaring makes every x² positive, so y is always positive. A branch below the x-axis belongs to y = 1/x, not 1/x².

b.q: Sam graphs y = √x. Which x-value gives no point on the graph?
b.why: The square root of a negative number is not a real number, so the graph has no point for x = −4. The value x = 0 is tempting, but it is allowed and gives the start point (0, 0).
b.clue: Which x-value would put a negative number under the root?

a.best: It has the y-axis as an asymptote and lies above the x-axis

final.title: Power functions
card: A power function has the form \(y = x^{n}\), where \(n\) can be negative or a fraction. Its graph is shaped by values it cannot reach.

\(x\) cannot be 0, so the y-axis is a vertical asymptote, a line the graph approaches but never touches. \(y = 0\) is a horizontal asymptote. For \(y = \frac{1}{x}\) the branches are in opposite quadrants. For \(y = \frac{1}{x^{2}}\) both branches are above the x-axis.
\(y = \sqrt{x}\) needs \(x \ge 0\), so the graph starts at the point \((0, 0)\) and rises to the right. It has no part to the left of the y-axis.
Example: \(y = \frac{1}{x}\) has no point at \(x = 0\). When \(x = 2\), \(y = \frac{1}{2}\). When \(x = -2\), \(y = -\frac{1}{2}\).

2.alt: The graphs of \(y = \frac{1}{x}\) and \(y = \frac{1}{x^{2}}\). Neither has a point at \(x = 0\), and both get closer to the y-axis and the x-axis without touching them. \(y = \frac{1}{x}\) has one branch in the top right and one in the bottom left. \(y = \frac{1}{x^{2}}\) has both branches above the x-axis.

3.alt: The graph of \(y = \sqrt{x}\). It starts at the origin, \((0, 0)\), and rises to the right through \((4, 2)\). It has no part to the left of the y-axis, because \(x\) cannot be negative.

final.remember: The values a power function cannot use, such as \(x = 0\) for \(\frac{1}{x}\) or negative \(x\) for \(\sqrt{x}\), set its shape.

a.q: Which statement is true for the graph of \(y = \frac{1}{x^{2}}\)?
opts: It has the y-axis as an asymptote and lies above the x-axis
It has the y-axis as an asymptote and dips below the x-axis
It passes through the origin and lies above the x-axis
It starts at the origin and has no part for negative \(x\)
a.why: \(x = 0\) is not allowed, so the y-axis is an asymptote. Squaring makes every \(x^{2}\) positive, so \(y\) is always positive. A branch below the x-axis belongs to \(y = \frac{1}{x}\), not \(y = \frac{1}{x^{2}}\).

b.q: Sam graphs \(y = \sqrt{x}\). Which x-value gives no point on the graph?
b.why: The square root of a negative number is not a real number, so the graph has no point for \(x = -4\). The value \(x = 0\) is tempting, but it is allowed and gives the start point \((0, 0)\).
b.clue: Which x-value would put a negative number under the root?
